paragraphs.heading: The thick middle layer
paragraphs.text: The mantle is the layer of silicate rock between Earth's crust and its outer core. It is about 2,900 kilometres thick, roughly 46% of Earth's radius. Although it is mostly solid, over geologic time it flows like a very thick fluid, and it is sometimes compared to caramel.

paragraphs.heading: Layers within the mantle
paragraphs.text: The top of the mantle is marked by a sudden jump in seismic velocity, first noticed by Andrija Mohorovičić in 1909 and now called the Moho. The upper mantle has two main layers: a rigid top part, the lithospheric mantle, and the more ductile asthenosphere below it. Together with the crust above, the lithospheric mantle forms the lithosphere, which makes up the tectonic plates that move over the asthenosphere. Under the oceans the lithosphere is about 100 km thick, and under continents it is usually 150–200 km. Below the asthenosphere, the mantle is fairly rigid again.

paragraphs.heading: What it is made of
paragraphs.text: The upper mantle is mostly peridotite, a rock made largely of olivine, two kinds of pyroxene and an aluminium-bearing mineral. At the top of the transition zone, olivine changes into the high-pressure forms wadsleyite and ringwoodite without changing its chemistry. Unlike olivine, these forms can store a lot of water in their crystals, which is one reason to think the transition zone may hold a large amount of water. At the base of that zone, ringwoodite breaks down into bridgmanite and ferropericlase, the main minerals of the lower mantle.

paragraphs.heading: Hot but solid
paragraphs.text: Temperatures run from about 500 K where the mantle meets the crust to about 4,200 K at the boundary with the core. That is far hotter than the roughly 1,500 K at which typical mantle rock, peridotite, melts at the surface, yet the mantle stays almost entirely solid. The reason is pressure: the temperature at which melting begins rises as pressure rises. Pressure climbs from a few hundred megapascals at the Moho to 139 GPa at the core-mantle boundary.

paragraphs.heading: Slow circulation
paragraphs.text: Because the surface and the outer core differ in temperature, and because hot rock under high pressure can creep slowly over millions of years, material circulates through the mantle. Hot material rises in plumes while cooler, heavier material sinks, and the sinking happens at subduction zones, where plates converge. Ground above a plume is expected to stand high, since the hot plume beneath is buoyant, and to have hot spot volcanoes. Another explanation for that volcanism is that the crust stretches and lets magma leak to the surface, an idea called the plate hypothesis.

paragraphs.heading: Hidden zones and rare samples
paragraphs.text: Seismic images reveal two continent-sized zones at the bottom of the mantle where seismic velocities are low. They are denser than the rock around them and probably differ in makeup. One idea is that they are leftover mantle material from Theia, buried after the Moon-forming event described by the giant-impact hypothesis. Because the mantle is mostly out of reach, its makeup is hard to pin down. Rare samples come from ophiolites, where slices of ocean lithosphere have been pushed onto a continent, and from xenoliths, fragments of mantle rock caught up in basalt or kimberlite as it forms.
